doc: The question and answer texts INIT (run C, ref 0b6efce) was trained on, for ml/c3/desc_gate.py on a copy with no git history.
texts: What it is. Which type is this line, or which kind of noise? What kind of fact the line states.
physical site: Authoritative site declaration: site_id + facility name + street address. One per real building / location.
site attribute: A scalar attribute of a site: user count, room count, square feet, priority, floors.
site access restriction: A constraint on access: blackout window, restricted hours, badged escort required, weekend-only cutover, etc.
site room mix: A row from a per-site room-mix table: room type + count + standard build + validation test.
site infrastructure: Site-bound infrastructure facts: MDF/IDF id, bandwidth/circuit, cable plant condition.

derived finding: A statement nobody wrote: counted, measured or noticed-to-be-absent by the parser from an artifact's own structure -- 106 workstations counted as CAD block inserts, 828 ft of new partition summed from linework, a telecom layer noticed missing. Carries what it assumed and what it decides, because a derived claim has to be arguable.

deal state: Where the deal stands, derived from its own sentences rather than written by anyone: the step it waits on, who owns that step, and whether its price has been checked against the site. Consolidates the coordination traffic -- scheduling, acknowledgements, chasing -- that moves a deal but never reaches a SOW.
service line: A services-row line item: service id + description + unit + qty + unit price + extended cost.
bom line: A hardware-BOM table row: item id + description + SKU + qty + unit price + extended cost + lead time + serial-capture flag.
payment term: One row of a billing/payment schedule, e.g. '30% at order acceptance'. Each tier is its own atom.
commercial total: An aggregate price line: hardware subtotal, services subtotal, freight/logistics, contingency, taxes, grand total. Each is one atom.
pricing assumption: An explicit pricing assumption or rate term (taxes excluded, hardware substitutions require approval, after-hours work billed at 150% of the standard rate, etc.).
site budget: Per-site budget category amount (hardware budget / services budget / logistics estimate per site).
rate card: A priced rate table row: role or service with a bill rate, OT/holiday multiplier, minimum hours.
work scope item: A general statement of work to be performed that is not a discrete task, deliverable or requirement.

deal summary: THE line the whole deal can be read from: service, quantity, site and deal type in one sentence -- "4 TVs install in CheckOut New York office." At most one per deal. Not every scope line -- a work_scope_item says one thing the job includes; this says what the job IS. Proposed on 010087.
requirement: A formally numbered requirement (REQ-001 style) with applies-to + owner + verification method.

task: Billable work we will perform for the customer on this job -- the labor the quote prices. It is written as the customer's request for our work or for a technician's time ('install and set up two devices at the site', 'looking for a partner to install their new display', 'please quote a technician onsite for 2-3 hours to get the register and printer running'), as a statement of what will be set up or installed on the job ('we will be setting 1 register and 1 kitchen printer', '3 Verkada cameras install', 'Relocate 10 APs to 15 ft', 'Conduct the site survey'), or as a row from a detailed-task table (task_id + site + phase + description + owner + dates + dependency + status). Our own sales and office steps (quoting, scheduling, onboarding, invoicing, account setup) are not tasks: _keep. Work the customer or a third party will do (send floor plans, provide access, ship equipment) is a dependency. A remark or plan to check something, a question about the site, a call summary of what was agreed, a description of the site as it is, or a quantity or date alone is not a task: _keep.
deliverable: A named deliverable that a phase produces (e.g. 'Network closet readiness checklist').
acceptance criterion: A row from an acceptance-criteria table — area + criteria + pass threshold.
milestone phase: A row from a project phase/milestone table — phase number + name + start date + end date + owner + exit criteria. Synonyms accepted: phase, sprint, wave, milestone, stage.
cutover step: A row from a cutover/runbook checklist — step number + timing relative to cutover + owner + action + evidence required.
electrical acceptance test: A measurable electrical/network acceptance test (Megger, ground resistance, load burn-in, witness/ATP).
site implementation note: Site-specific implementation instruction (asset-tag prefix, receiving rule, install rule).
site access window: When a site is accessible — days + hours + escort owner.
exclusion: Negative scope: something explicitly NOT included ("electrical by others", "no patching").
integration checkpoint: A row from a system-to-system integration checkpoint table: checkpoint id + system + expected input/output + owner + due.
data flow step: One step of a data-flow pipeline (source system → sink system, what payload).
system mapping: A field mapping between two systems (e.g.
mitigation: A mitigation paired with a specific risk (separate from the risk atom itself).
constraint: A limit on how the work may be done: working hours, noise, dust, union labor, escort required.
compliance rule: A rule about access, data handling, retention, credential use, or auditing.
compliance classification: A document/data classification + its allowed and blocked destinations (Confidential, Internal, Mock, Production).
approval authority: A rule that some role/threshold requires a specific approver (e.g. 'CFO signoff required over $1.5M').
submission req: A required element of the proposal submission: number of copies, file format, required form (SF330, W-9), page limit, sealed-bid labeling, delivery method.

change order rule: A rule that governs change orders — when one is required, T&M rate caps, materials markup, the rate for change-order work. A standing rate term (after-hours billed at 150%) is a pricing_assumption.
bonding insurance: A bonding or insurance requirement: bid bond, performance bond, payment bond, general liability limit, workers comp, professional liability.
contract term: A contractual term governing the resulting agreement: contract length, renewal/option years, payment terms (net 30), warranty period, retainage, liquidated-damages clause reference.
certification: A certification or credential the provider or its technicians must hold (e.g. BICSI RCDD, OSHA-10, manufacturer cert).
stakeholder: A named person on the deal with their role and email. Synonyms accepted: owner, lead, sponsor, accountable, contact.
blackout date range: A no-work date window (holiday freeze, exec blackout, peak travel exclusion).
lead time constraint: Lead time + expediting policy for an item class (core switches, APs, AV kits, fiber panels, custom millwork).
deadline: A hard date/time the bidder must meet: proposal/bid due date, questions-due date, pre-bid meeting, site visit. NOT a project phase end (that is milestone_phase).
dependency: A dependency on a customer-provided input, third party, or infrastructure readiness.
deal metadata: Header-level fact about the deal itself: customer name, deal ID, quote/PO/MSA references, contract type, currency, target close date, deal stage.

source caveat: A fact about a SOURCE DOCUMENT that changes how it must be read: who produced it, which part of it is wrong, what supersedes it, what it is out of date against. Not scope -- it must never reach the SOW -- and it must travel WITH the document it is about, because anything that reads that document without it builds from something we already know is wrong. Found in 11 deals across the dev corpus, typed scope_item in 9 of them: "the Dates are incorrect as per the submitted SOW", "except as otherwise superseded by terms contained in a mutually executed Master Purchase Agreement".

legend entry: The key that makes a document decodable: what a colour, symbol, hatch or abbreviation MEANS on the sheet it is printed on ("Huzzard supplied Components", "orange = existing", "hatched = by others"). Not a fact about the work and never scope -- its content transfers into the parts it governs, each of which names the side it was drawn in. It exists as an atom so a correction can point AT it: on 010288 the sender writes "the 'Installer Supplied Components' are not accurate", and a caveat aimed at a whole drawing says only that the drawing is unreliable, while one aimed at a single key says which eighteenth of it to distrust. Distinct from source_caveat, which is the correction rather than the thing corrected.

list header: A pointer line that introduces a list and says nothing on its own: "Locations:", "The following items are excluded:". Its meaning lives in the items under it, which carry it as their lead-in. Not _keep -- the list it names is real -- and not the type of the items it introduces.
eval criterion: A scored evaluation/award criterion with its weight: 'Technical approach 40%', 'Price 30%', 'Past performance 20%'. One per criterion.
approval decision: A recorded approval/conditional approval/rejection statement by a named stakeholder.
metadata requirement: A required metadata key/value to set on an object (blob metadata, CRM custom field).
signatory: A signature-block entry — role + named person who signs.
addendum qa: An addendum, amendment, or question-and-answer item issued during the solicitation that modifies or clarifies the original documents.
site allocation: Per-site qty breakdown of a single BOM line (e.g. 'HW-001: ATL-HQ:52; ATL-WEST:27; ATL-AIR:15').
scope item: Legacy catch-all for a line of scope. Prefer a finer type; use only when none fits.
risk: A stated risk or concern that could affect delivery, cost or schedule.
assumption: Something the proposal assumes to be true ("customer provides lift", "pathways exist").
open question: An unanswered question in the documents that someone must resolve.
decision: A decision already made and recorded ("customer chose option B").
action item: A to-do assigned to a person, usually from meeting notes or email.
vendor line item: A vendor quote/BOM line: part, quantity, price.
customer instruction: A direct instruction from the customer about how to do the work.
quantity: A bare count of a thing ("110 TVs", "24 drops") not attached to a line item.
entity: A named thing (company, product, person) with no claim attached.
answered question: A question together with its answer, in the same message or a later reply ("How many doors?" / "1 external door"). The answer is the fact; keep both.
internal question: A question between people on our own team (routing, who to ask, pricing among ourselves). Never a question for the customer.
commitment: Someone promises to do something ("we will send the floorplan Friday", "I will get a conversation going with the owner").

small talk: Relationship talk that carries no fact about the work: thanks, greetings, banter, "sending this to my team". If the line ALSO says something about the job (its size, a document we need, a promise), it is not small talk.
keep: Not a fact worth typing: boilerplate, headers, signatures, table scaffolding, legal footer. The parser should drop or ignore it.

What it is. Which type is this line, or which kind of noise? Just relationship talk. Thanks, greetings, banter. NOT small talk if it also says anything about the work, promises something, or names a person or a document.
What it is. Which type is this line, or which kind of noise? What kind of noise. Only on _keep and small_talk rows: which kind of line carries no fact for anyone.
What kind of noise: not this kind of line
What kind of noise: greeting thanks. A hello, thank you or similar pleasantry.
What kind of noise: banter reassurance. Friendly chat or reassurance with no fact in it ("no worries, we've got you").
What kind of noise: signoff wrapper. A sign-off, signature block or the lines around one.
What kind of noise: legal footer. A confidentiality notice, disclaimer or other legal footer.
What kind of noise: automated wrapper. Text a system added around the message: forwarded headers, notification shells, tracking lines.
What kind of noise: table scaffolding. A table's empty cells, ruling or repeated headers with no value of their own.
What kind of noise: section heading. A heading with no fact of its own and nothing below it to govern.
What kind of noise: attachment pointer. A line that only says a file is attached, with no content of its own.
What kind of noise: speech filler. Filler words from a call transcript ("um", "yeah, so").
What kind of noise: page chrome. Page numbers, running headers, footers and other print furniture.
What kind of noise: template instruction. An instruction to whoever fills in a template ("insert site name here").
What kind of noise: cross reference. A pointer to another part of the document ("see section 4") with no fact of its own.
What it is. Which type is this line, or which kind of noise? Which section of a project brief does this line belong in?
Brief section: not this kind of line
Brief section: WORK. What is done: the work itself.
Brief section: SITE. Where: the places and their conditions.
Brief section: COMMERCIAL. Money and terms.
Brief section: COMPLIANCE. Rules, insurance, safety and paperwork.
Brief section: PARTY. Who: the people and companies.
Brief section: TIMING. When: dates, windows and order.
Brief section: META. About the documents themselves.

Whose fact, and what it wants. Whose fact is it, what does it ask of us, who supplies it, and does it bring someone in? Whose fact is it? The type says WHAT a statement is; this says what it is ABOUT. Only 'deal' reaches the SOW -- 'account' and 'partner' belong in the brief's why-you-should-care, and are lost entirely if a labeler is forced to call them scope. See _LABELING_DOCTRINE.md.
about: not this kind of line
about: deal. This job. This quote, this scope, this site. The only one that reaches the SOW.
about: account. The customer relationship. True beyond this job: room to grow, who decides, how they buy.
about: partner. A partner's behaviour. How a reseller, vendor or installer works with us -- their drawings, their terms, what they get wrong.
about: internal. How we work. Our own routing and process. Never a deliverable.

Whose fact, and what it wants. Whose fact is it, what does it ask of us, who supplies it, and does it bring someone in? What does this statement want from us? Turns 'there is something we are missing' into a list someone can work. See _LABELING_DOCTRINE.md.
wants: not this kind of line
wants: nothing. Nothing — it is just true. The line is simply true; nobody has to fetch, ask or decide anything.
wants: chase artifact. Go get a document. It points at a drawing, quote or photo the deal does not hold.
wants: chase conversation. Find the conversation. It refers to a call or thread we do not have ("as discussed earlier").
wants: confirm with customer. Ask the customer. We cannot price or build it until they answer.
wants: decide internally. We must decide. Nobody else can answer it; it is our call to make.
Whose fact, and what it wants. Whose fact is it, what does it ask of us, who supplies it, and does it bring someone in?
supplier: not this kind of line
supplier: us. The service provider writing the quote supplies or does it.
supplier: partner. Partner / reseller. A reseller or partner working with the provider supplies or does it.
supplier: customer. End customer. The end customer supplies or does it.
supplier: third party. Another vendor. Another vendor or contractor outside the deal's main parties supplies or does it.

supplier: unresolved. Named but not resolved. The document names a ROLE and not an organisation -- "Provided by Club/installer" when we are the installer, so it means the club or us. Leaving it blank reads as "not answered"; this says the deal does not say, which is a finding and usually an unpriced cost.

Whose fact, and what it wants. Whose fact is it, what does it ask of us, who supplies it, and does it bring someone in? Brings in someone not in this thread. A decision maker, landlord, installer or facilities manager being brought into the deal. Write the role alone when nobody named them ("club owner") -- that absence IS the finding, because we cannot contact a role.
Brings in someone not in this thread: the line does not say
Brings in someone not in this thread: the line says it

Whose fact, and what it wants. Whose fact is it, what does it ask of us, who supplies it, and does it bring someone in? Matters here, generalises nowhere. Worth keeping for anyone reading THIS deal and worth no rule at all. Not a fact about the work, not pure boilerplate: the acknowledgement that explains why a second message arrived, the forward that says who now holds the job, the aside that only means something next to the line above it. Say what it is doing HERE -- "explains why the address came separately" -- never just that it is minor. `_keep` deletes a line; this one preserves it without teaching anything, which is the whole difference. A head should come away from it with nothing.
Matters here, generalises nowhere: the line does not say
Matters here, generalises nowhere: the line says it

The facts it states. Which entity is it about, and which value does it give: size, quantity, date, billing basis, option? How big the sender thinks it is. Sizing in the sender's own words, before any site visit.
How big the sender thinks it is: not this kind of line
How big the sender thinks it is: small. The sender calls the job small, quick or simple, or sizes it at a handful of devices, rooms or hours, before anyone has walked the site.
How big the sender thinks it is: large. The sender calls the job large, a full build-out or a multi-phase project, or sizes it at many sites, floors or days, before anyone has walked the site.

The facts it states. Which entity is it about, and which value does it give: size, quantity, date, billing basis, option? What the cell is in a BOM row. The role of this value in its bill-of-materials row: part number, description, quantity, unit_price, ext_price, and so on.
What the cell is in a BOM row: the line does not say
What the cell is in a BOM row: the line says it

The facts it states. Which entity is it about, and which value does it give: size, quantity, date, billing basis, option? What kind of scope line. The universal kind of scope line. A company's own SOW group name goes in scope_category.
What kind of scope line: not this kind of line
What kind of scope line: summary. A one-line summary of the whole job or a whole phase.
What kind of scope line: work step. One task the crew performs, such as mount, run, terminate or configure.
What kind of scope line: schedule. When the work happens or how long it takes.
What kind of scope line: tooling. Tools, lifts or equipment the crew needs to do the work.
What kind of scope line: materials. The parts and materials installed or consumed.
What kind of scope line: staffing. How many people, which skills and how many visits.
What kind of scope line: testing. Tests, certification or verification of the work.
What kind of scope line: documentation. Drawings, as-builts, photos, reports or labels handed over.
What kind of scope line: responsibility. Who does what, said as a split of duties.
What kind of scope line: exclusion. Something the job leaves out.
What kind of scope line: other. A scope line that fits none of the kinds above.

The facts it states. Which entity is it about, and which value does it give: size, quantity, date, billing basis, option? The option is ticked. On a checkbox or option line: whether it was selected. Ticked or not, the line is a fact.
The option is ticked: not marked

The facts it states. Which entity is it about, and which value does it give: size, quantity, date, billing basis, option? When the work starts. The line sets or proposes when on-site work begins: "see you Friday at 9am". Copy the date and time as said. Label the confirmed start once, on the line that confirms it; an earlier proposal that changed is superseded by it.
When the work starts: the line does not say
When the work starts: the line says it

The facts it states. Which entity is it about, and which value does it give: size, quantity, date, billing basis, option? How the work is billed. The pricing basis a line states: one fixed price, time and materials (units times a rate, so every total is an estimate), milestone payments, or a price per site (a unit times the site count). Same values as the deal-level billing judgment.
How the work is billed: not this kind of line
How the work is billed: fixed. One fixed price for the stated scope, whatever the hours turn out to be.
How the work is billed: t and m. Time and materials: hours or units times a rate, so any total is an estimate.
How the work is billed: milestone. Payments tied to stages of the work, such as a deposit, a mid-point payment and a payment on completion.
How the work is billed: per site. A price per site, multiplied by the number of sites.

The facts it states. Which entity is it about, and which value does it give: size, quantity, date, billing basis, option? Display size. The screen size the line states: "75 inch" is 75. Size sets how many techs a mount takes.
Display size: the line does not say
Display size: the line says it

The facts it states. Which entity is it about, and which value does it give: size, quantity, date, billing basis, option? How many units. The count of displays, devices or units the line states. A count of sites is job_scale; a count of people is crew_size.
How many units: the line does not say
How many units: the line says it

The facts it states. Which entity is it about, and which value does it give: size, quantity, date, billing basis, option? What kind of requirement. What the line requires, in a word or two (access, hardware, labor, permit, schedule...). Open set for now.
What kind of requirement: the line does not say
What kind of requirement: the line says it

The facts it states. Which entity is it about, and which value does it give: size, quantity, date, billing basis, option? Material named. A material or consumable the line names (cable, mounts, conduit), in its own words.
Material named: the line does not say
Material named: the line says it

The facts it states. Which entity is it about, and which value does it give: size, quantity, date, billing basis, option? Whose side of the scope. Who the line puts the work or item on: the provider doing the job, the customer, a third party, or both.
Whose side of the scope: not this kind of line
Whose side of the scope: provider. The service provider doing the job does the work or brings the item.
Whose side of the scope: customer. The end customer does the work or supplies the item themselves.
Whose side of the scope: third party. Someone outside the provider and the customer does it, such as another contractor, the landlord, a carrier or a manufacturer.
Whose side of the scope: shared. Two or more parties split it, and the line says or implies each side's part.
The facts it states. Which entity is it about, and which value does it give: size, quantity, date, billing basis, option? Which site. The site the line is about, by the name the text uses.
Which site: the line does not say
Which site: the line says it
The facts it states. Which entity is it about, and which value does it give: size, quantity, date, billing basis, option? Where it is. The address or place the line gives, verbatim.
Where it is: the line does not say
Where it is: the line says it

The facts it states. Which entity is it about, and which value does it give: size, quantity, date, billing basis, option? A rate the line states. A price per unit of work the text gives ("$95/hr", "$920 per day"). Whether it is our rate or theirs is policy, not this reading.
A rate the line states: the line does not say
A rate the line states: the line says it

The facts it states. Which entity is it about, and which value does it give: size, quantity, date, billing basis, option? What the rate is for. The work or role the stated rate applies to ("lead tech", "after-hours").
What the rate is for: the line does not say
What the rate is for: the line says it

Its place in the document. What kind of document is it in, which section, and is it the deal's own words or template? What kind of document it comes from. The document's own kind (quote, BOM, SOW, floor plan, email), beyond the file type.
What kind of document it comes from: the line does not say
What kind of document it comes from: the line says it

Its place in the document. What kind of document is it in, which section, and is it the deal's own words or template? Filled in or still the template. On a SOW line: the deal's own words (filled), the template's placeholder text left as is (template), or standard template wording that still sets a real term for this deal (template_applies).
Filled in or still the template: not this kind of line
Filled in or still the template: filled. The SOW line carries this deal's own facts: names, counts, dates or sites written for this job.
Filled in or still the template: template. The SOW line is the template's placeholder or boilerplate left as it was, not written for this deal.
Filled in or still the template: template applies. The SOW line is standard template wording, but it still sets a real term for this deal, such as a rate uplift, a minimum or a cancellation fee.

Its place in the document. What kind of document is it in, which section, and is it the deal's own words or template? Which SOW section it belongs in. The standard SOW section this line lands in. overview is the introduction, executive summary or project overview; acceptance is how the work is accepted; change_control is how scope changes are requested and priced; terms is termination and the other legal terms. provider_responsibilities is the service provider's side; no company name belongs in the value.
Which SOW section it belongs in: not this kind of line
Which SOW section it belongs in: overview. The introduction, executive summary or project overview: what the project is and why.
Which SOW section it belongs in: scope of work. The work to be done: tasks, quantities and where.
Which SOW section it belongs in: deliverables. What is handed over at the end: equipment in place, documents, drawings or test results.
Which SOW section it belongs in: acceptance. How the work is accepted as complete: the criteria, tests or sign-off.
Which SOW section it belongs in: out of scope. What the job explicitly does not include.
Which SOW section it belongs in: assumptions. What the price and plan assume to be true, such as access, existing conditions or working hours.
Which SOW section it belongs in: customer responsibilities. What the customer must do or provide.
Which SOW section it belongs in: provider responsibilities. What the service provider must do or provide beyond the listed tasks.
Which SOW section it belongs in: timeline. Dates, durations, phases and the order of the work.
Which SOW section it belongs in: fees. Prices, rates, payment terms and invoicing.
Which SOW section it belongs in: change control. How changes to the scope are requested, priced and approved.
Which SOW section it belongs in: terms. Termination and the other legal terms: liability, warranty, governing law.
Which SOW section it belongs in: contacts. Who the people are and how to reach them.
Which SOW section it belongs in: other. A real SOW line that fits none of the sections above.

Its place in the document. What kind of document is it in, which section, and is it the deal's own words or template? How the value was arrived at. stated: the text says it. inferred: it follows from the text and trade knowledge. template: it came from a template default. not_derivable: nothing on the page supports it.
How the value was arrived at: not this kind of line
How the value was arrived at: stated. The text says the value outright.
How the value was arrived at: inferred. The value follows from the text plus trade knowledge, but the text does not say it.
How the value was arrived at: template. The value came from a template default, not from this deal.
How the value was arrived at: not derivable. Nothing on the page supports the value.

Its place in the document. What kind of document is it in, which section, and is it the deal's own words or template? Which part of it must not be trusted. Name the section, legend or column that is wrong -- "Installer Supplied Components" -- not just that something is. This is the reading that has to be carried down into the analysis of the document: a caveat nobody can act on is a caveat nobody applies.
Which part of it must not be trusted: the line does not say
Which part of it must not be trusted: the line says it

Its place in the document. What kind of document is it in, which section, and is it the deal's own words or template? Names a document. The line refers to a drawing or file, whether or not we hold it.
Names a document: the line does not say
Names a document: the line says it

Its place in the document. What kind of document is it in, which section, and is it the deal's own words or template? A template placeholder. The line is an unfilled template slot ("[Customer Name]", "TBD") rather than a fact.

How the job is billed: not this kind of line
How the job is billed: fixed. One fixed price.
How the job is billed: t and m. Time and materials: billed for hours and parts used.

Consumables: not this kind of line
Consumables: consumables. Yes, consumables are in scope.
The deal as a whole. What is this deal mainly, and what did the parser get wrong across it? Are expenses (shipping, per diem, freight) billed on this job?
Expenses: not this kind of line
Expenses: expenses. Yes, expenses are billed.
The deal as a whole. What is this deal mainly, and what did the parser get wrong across it? Is travel (mileage, airfare, hotel, drive time) billed on this job?
Travel: not this kind of line
Travel: travel. Yes, travel is billed.
Which atoms exist. Should this text be an atom at all, did the parser form it right, and when it lost a line, why?
admission: not this kind of line
admission: keep. keep: a real fact about the work, worth an atom
admission: drop. drop: not a fact; wreckage, boilerplate, small talk or a torn fragment

Which atoms exist. Should this text be an atom at all, did the parser form it right, and when it lost a line, why? Why the parser lost the line. Only on a line added by hand (a Missed row, origin labeler): what the parse did that left the line with no atom of its own. It stays on the row as history after a later parse produces the line.
Why the parser lost the line: not this kind of line
Why the parser lost the line: glued paragraph. A fact sentence sat inside a paragraph the parser cut as a whole (a greeting or chatter paragraph), so the fact went with it.
Why the parser lost the line: table cell glued. A table cell's parts ran together, or the cell was read with no atom of its own.
Why the parser lost the line: table row dropped. A table row produced no atom, or only a fragment of one.
Why the parser lost the line: heading as section. A heading was used only as the section path of the lines under it and never became a line.
Why the parser lost the line: checkbox cell. A grid's tick-box cell was read as decoration.
Why the parser lost the line: folded copy. A dedup fold removed the only copy of the line under its own parent.

Only PM, PC, SA or tech work counts: sellers do not get tasks from this. seller, customer, partner and other say who owns it when it is none of the delivery roles; which owners a company plans work for is that company's policy.
Whose task it is: not this kind of line
Whose task it is: project manager. The project manager who runs the job day to day: schedule, budget and customer updates.

Whose task it is: solutions architect. The technical designer who scopes the system, draws it and answers how it should be built.
Whose task it is: technician. The technician on site who installs, tests and documents the work.
Whose task it is: seller. The salesperson or account manager who sold the deal.
Whose task it is: customer. Someone on the customer's side owns the task.
Whose task it is: partner. A reseller, vendor or other contractor owns the task.

Name the event in the line's own words ("TVs confirmed on site"). Link the event's atom with triggered_by when it arrives, the dependency with blocked_by, and the task with context. A seller saying they will reply or send something is not a task for us.
